title: The Antarctic Treaty
text:
In the 1950s Antarctica was a potential flashpoint. Seven countries claimed slices of it, some of them overlapping, and both the United States and the Soviet Union reserved the right to make claims of their own. Military interest was growing.

Then scientists took the lead. During the International Geophysical Year, from July 1957 to the end of 1958, researchers from dozens of nations carried out coordinated studies of the Earth. Twelve countries set up dozens of research stations in Antarctica, including American and Soviet bases deep in the interior. In the middle of the Cold War, the scientists shared data, visited each other's stations and sometimes exchanged personnel.

The success of this cooperation led to a conference in Washington. On 1 December 1959 the twelve nations active in Antarctica signed the Antarctic Treaty. It declared that the continent would be used for peaceful purposes only, and banned military bases, maneuvers and weapons tests. It banned nuclear explosions and the disposal of radioactive waste there. It froze all territorial claims, guaranteed freedom of scientific research, and required the exchange of plans and results. Any signatory could send observers to inspect any station at any time.

The treaty came into force in 1961. It was one of the first arms control agreements of the Cold War. Today dozens of countries are parties to it, and Antarctica remains a continent set aside for science and peace.
lesson: Cooperation at the working level can build the trust that formal agreements need. Shared projects can open a door that diplomacy alone cannot.
people: Twelve signatory nations, scientists of the International Geophysical Year
source: The Antarctic Treaty (1959); records of the International Geophysical Year
